{"item": 8, "draw": "stage2-control-d1", "call": 460, "article": "[Item] id gnews:cb05b9f49943ef0ba412cf36, category T8, author futuriom.com (analyst), published 2026-07-08, title: What's Up with NVIDIA's Latest Financial Model?\n\nWhat's Up with NVIDIA's Latest Financial Model?\nNVIDIA shares tumbled on recent news that the vendor will guarantee the sale of GPU capacity for selected AI cloud providers (aka neoclouds) over several years. In return, NVIDIA will share in revenues earned above the guaranteed, or backstop, level.\nThe point of this new model is to allow what NVIDIA terms “startups, model builders, enterprises, research organizations and regional AI players” access to better terms from neocloud service providers.\nUp to now, those cloud providers have been demanding contracts of long duration to sustain their own spending. With NVIDIA backing them up, these cloud providers will get better terms from their creditors. In turn, they can afford to offer shorter-term contracts to smaller organizations that have cash but lack the capital to buy the infrastructure they need.\nIn other words, instead of foregoing expensive neocloud services to get the GPU power they require, startups and other smaller-than-hyperscaler organizations can get those services without having to build their own infrastructure.\nHere’s how NVIDIA CFO Colette Kress and VP of Global AI Clouds and Infrastructure Ecosystem Raj Mirpuri described it in their joint announcement blog:\n“This new model enables AI clouds to procure NVIDIA infrastructure for AI-native, enterprise and ISV customers through economic alignment with a revenue-sharing and credit-support model. Through the partnership, AI clouds will sell NVIDIA-powered cloud services, with NVIDIA earning both standard product revenue and a share of the cloud revenue on the supported capacity. This structure accelerates adoption of NVIDIA platforms among the high-growth, high-conviction AI native sector, and provides NVIDIA with a recurring, usage-linked earnings stream.\n“For model builders, inference providers, agent platforms and enterprises scaling AI, it can mean faster access to full-stack accelerated computing without waiting through site selection, power procurement, construction and hardware bring-up.”\nNVIDIA states that two AI cloud providers have already signed on for the new deal: Sharon AI, based in Australia, will buy up to 40,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs under the plan. Firmus, based in Indoesia, is building a DSX AI factory there that’s expected to scale to 360 megawatts and contain up to 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs.\nThere is a precedent to the new NVIDIA model. NVIDIA reportedly has had a backstop deal with CoreWeave since 2023, in which it has agreed to pay up to $6.3 billion through 2032 if the cloud provider fails to sell a specified amount of NVIDIA GPU capacity.\nIt all sounds great, doesn’t it? Everyone benefits—the service provider, the end customer, and NVIDIA. So why did NVIDIA’s stock tank the day of the announcement?\nIt seems that investors aren’t entirely convinced that NVIDIA is right about AI compute demand. After all, some say, the hyperscalers are selling spare GPU capacity they themselves can’t use, implying that they’ve overbuilt their AI factories.\nOn July 1, the same day NVIDIA announced its new revenue-sharing model, Bloomberg reported that Meta is setting up a cloud-based business selling AI compute and models. If Meta, which planned to buy “millions” of GPUs from NVIDIA earlier this year, now doesn’t need those chips, what does that say about AI demand? Consider how NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang described Meta at the time:\n“No one deploys AI at Meta’s scale—integrating frontier research with industrial-scale infrastructure to power the world’s largest personalization and recommendation systems for billions of users.”\nApparently, that enormous demand has been met, turning investors skeptical about the ongoing scale of hyperscaler AI infrastructure—and by association, the scale of AI demand in general.\nMore Circularity?\nNVIDIA’s latest financial model also points to investor concerns that NVIDIA tends to circularity in its dealings. Investing in CoreWeave , for instance, has provided NVIDIA infrastructure to customers such as OpenAI, in which NVIDIA has also invested . Revenue sharing with cloud providers also pays NVIDIA for selling its own chips. The complex, circular nature of these deals is one of several concerns about NVIDIA raised by investors over the past few months.\nNVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has called these concerns “ridiculous,\" and he maintains the ongoing need for GPU power: \"Without compute, there's no way to generate tokens. Without tokens, there's no way to grow revenues. In this new world of AI, compute equals revenues,\" he said on the Q4 FY2026 earnings call in February 2026.\nNevertheless, doubts persist. NVIDIA’s stock also suffered this week because research firm SemiAnalysis stated in an X post that NVIDIA’s Kyber NVL144 rack system has hit manufacturing setbacks—a situation that could be further impetus for NVIDIA to deploy its new credit and revenue-sharing model, creating a continuing flow of demand for its products.\nAn NVIDIA spokesperson said, “Our road map is intact.” Further, \"Vera Rubin Ultra will scale up to a larger NVL576 domain in its planned 2027 timeline.\"\nFuturiom Take: NVIDIA’s new business model for AI cloud providers could boost demand for its GPUs among startups and other small enterprises. But investor doubts persist about the scale of AI demand and the circular nature of some of NVIDIA's arrangements. We’ll see what a few quarterly reports reveal.\nAs trillions of dollars of AI cloud infrastructure is deployed, new infrastructure efficiency will become the key to delivering a return on investment. ...", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["Sharon AI signed on to NVIDIA’s new AI-cloud model and plans to buy up to 40,000 Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs.", "Firmus is building a DSX AI factory in Indonesia expected to scale to 360 megawatts and contain up to 170,000 NVIDIA GPUs.", "Futuriom says NVIDIA’s new financial model adds to investor concerns about circularity in its dealings."], "ladder_as_the_judge_is_shown_it": {"object": "NVDA", "kind": "asset", "question": "What total amount of financing commitments and capacity backstops to customers and partners will NVIDIA report outstanding at its FY2027 year-end?", "year": "FY2027", "due_day": "2027-02-28", "rungs": [{"position": 1, "label": "Strongly bullish", "condition": "The reported total is at least $12 billion."}, {"position": 2, "label": "Bullish", "condition": "The reported total is at least $6 billion but less than $12 billion."}, {"position": 3, "label": "Neutral", "condition": "The reported total is at least $2 billion but less than $6 billion."}, {"position": 4, "label": "Bearish", "condition": "The reported total is greater than $0 but less than $2 billion."}, {"position": 5, "label": "Strongly bearish", "condition": "The reported total is $0."}]}, "refused_by_production_check": null}

{"item": 10, "draw": "stage2-control-d1", "call": 752, "article": "[Item] id gnews:07cf5835d106467db5448c13, category T8, author fool.com (analyst), published 2026-07-12, title: Nvidia Stock Is Losing to the Market in 2026. Time to Walk Away or Double Down?\n\nSince 2023, Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has been the stock to own. It crushed the market in 2023, 2024, and 2025. However, it's not looking so good in 2026.\nAs of this writing, Nvidia is up around 8.7% this year, while the market (as measured by the S&P 500 ) has risen 10.2%. That kind of underperformance is obviously disappointing to the countless Nvidia investors out there, and what makes it even more frustrating is that several other stocks, including rival Advanced Micro Devices , have had phenomenal years.\nSo, is it time to walk away from Nvidia and select a different artificial intelligence (AI) stock? Or is it time to double down on your investment in anticipation of a strong second half? Let's take a look.\nSince the AI arms race began in 2023, Nvidia's GPUs have led the way as the top computing option. Nvidia's GPUs and the products that support them dominate the data center sector and are the top choice for nearly every company involved in AI. This level of dominance helped propel Nvidia to become the world's largest company by market cap, but there are some challenges looming ahead.\nOne threat could come from AI hyperscalers specializing in computing chips, as custom AI chips are starting to become a popular option. However, these chips require a workload to be properly configured to maximize their abilities, and that's not always possible. So, GPUs will remain a popular option.\nWith how bad Nvidia's stock has performed in 2026 (at least compared to the last three years' performance), investors may be surprised to see its rapid growth rates. During its past quarter, Nvidia's revenue increased at an 85% clip. That's not all, either, as Wall Street analysts expect 96% growth during Q2. Nvidia is still rapidly growing, making it a worthy investment, so why has the stock performed so poorly?\nThe most likely reason is skepticism of the AI build-out. The market isn't keen on the AI hyperscalers spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI computing equipment, especially when a viable business hasn't been proven by any generative AI firm yet. However, Nvidia told investors last quarter that it expects AI hyperaccelerator spending to rise to over $1 trillion next year. I'm more inclined to believe Nvidia over the market's skepticism, as it likely has orders on the books for next year, so it can easily see the demand already.\nAs 2027 spending projections start to become apparent, I think Nvidia's stock will rally to close 2026. Nvidia: Meta Has Quietly Emerged as the Strongest Mega-Cap Alternative This Summer\nBoth Meta and NVIDIA delivered blowout quarters on the same AI wave, yet investors treated the two stocks very differently this summer. Very different investor treatment lately.\nAds Are Roaring at Meta. Data Centers Are Doing the Work at NVIDIA.\nMeta’s Family of Apps generated $55.91 billion, with ad impressions up 19% and price per ad up 12%. That is real pricing power on a base of 3.56 billion daily users. Mark Zuckerberg framed it plainly: “We had a milestone quarter with strong momentum across our apps and the release of our first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs.” Reality Labs still bled $4.03 billion, a reminder that the AI dream costs real cash.\nNVIDIA’s story is denser. Jensen Huang called it “the largest infrastructure expansion in human history.” Yet zero H20 chips shipped to China this quarter, versus $4.6 billion a year ago. That absence is now baked into forward numbers.\nBuyer of Shovels Turns Seller of Compute\nHere is the twist that reframes the whole quarter. Meta raised 2026 capex to $125 to $145 billion, then quietly launched Meta Compute, a service renting its excess internal AI capacity to external enterprises. {"item": 12, "draw": "stage2-control-d1", "call": 886, "article": "[Item] id gnews:e0e5ab6c2aced8d5a6a688a5, category T8, author 247wallst.com (analyst), published 2026-07-13, title: Broadcom and Marvell Are Bigger Threats to Nvidia Than You Know\n\nBy Rich Duprey\nBroadcom (AVGO) and Marvell (MRVL) design custom AI chips costing between $6 billion and $11 billion per gigawatt, compared to $19 billion for Nvidia GPU racks.\nHyperscalers will spend over $1 trillion on AI next year, with Google alone adding more compute than all four combined did in 2025.\nNvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) remains the undisputed leader of the AI chip market, but leadership and dominance are not the same thing. The next phase of the AI buildout is shifting from buying the fastest hardware available to lowering the cost of operating AI at hyperscale.\nAlphabet ( NASDAQ:GOOG ), Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ), Meta Platforms ( NASDAQ:META ), and Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT ) are all pursuing custom silicon alongside Nvidia’s GPUs because every percentage point of efficiency matters when spending tens of billions of dollars annually on AI infrastructure.\nThat trend doesn’t eliminate Nvidia’s advantage, but it does create a growing opportunity for the companies designing those custom chips—most notably Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) and Marvell Technology ( NASDAQ:MRVL ).\nThe Battle Is Moving From Training to Cost Efficiency\nNvidia still owns AI training. Its GPUs remain the gold standard for developing frontier models, and its CUDA software ecosystem continues to give it a competitive moat. But this is where the market is changing.\nOnce models are trained, they spend years handling inference — answering prompts, generating images, and powering AI applications. Those workloads don’t always require Nvidia’s most powerful processors. They often reward lower costs and higher efficiency instead. That is where application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, enter the picture.\nBroadcom has become the leading partner helping hyperscalers build custom AI accelerators, while Marvell has carved out a similar niche with customers including Amazon. Rather than selling chips under their own brands, they help cloud providers design silicon optimized for their own software and infrastructure.\nMorgan Stanley says hyperscalers continue to expand their investments in proprietary silicon to improve total cost of ownership and reduce dependence on merchant GPU suppliers.\nThe opportunity for Broadcom and Marvell is enormous. The analyst says Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta are forecast to spend over $1 trillion on AI infrastructure next year, adding 19.5 gigawatts (GW) of incremental compute capacity. In 2025, they added roughly 6.7 GW. Google alone will add 6.8 GW, or more than the hyperscalers did combined two years ago.\nThe $1 trillion AI infrastructure race is pivoting: training is out, and custom-built efficiency is in. See why the industry's 'Second Act' is making room for new leaders beyond Nvidia.\nThe Economics Are Becoming Harder to Ignore\nThe appeal of custom silicon comes down to dollars. Milk Road AI estimates that building one gigawatt of AI infrastructure using Broadcom- or Marvell-designed ASIC racks cost between $6 billion and $11 billion, compared with roughly $19 billion using Nvidia GB300-based racks. Under Vera Rubin, rack costs jump to $25 billion. It illustrates why hyperscalers are increasingly willing to invest years designing their own chips.\nSurprisingly, this isn’t an either-or decision for hyperscalers. Google continues developing Tensor Processing Units with Broadcom while still purchasing enormous numbers of Nvidia GPUs. Amazon follows a similar strategy with Trainium alongside Nvidia deployments.\nThat diversification gives cloud providers leverage in negotiations while matching the right chip to the right workload.\nNvidia Is Still Winning — But Watch the Suppliers\nGranted, Nvidia is hardly standing still. The company continues expanding beyond GPUs into networking, rack-scale systems, and software while opening technologies such as NVLink Fusion to custom silicon partners — including Marvell itself.\nThat said, investors sometimes underestimate where the fastest incremental growth may occur. Every new custom AI accelerator designed by Google, Meta, Amazon, or another hyperscaler creates another opportunity for Broadcom or Marvell. They benefit whether customers build proprietary chips instead of buying more off-the-shelf processors, and they are standing directly in the path of a massive $1 trillion spending tsunami.\nIn other words, Nvidia remains the king of AI compute, but Broadcom and Marvell are increasingly becoming the architects behind the industry’s second act.\nIn short, investors shouldn’t mistake Nvidia’s dominance for exclusivity. The AI infrastructure market is expanding so rapidly that multiple winners can emerge. Nvidia still commands the premium end of AI computing, particularly for training, but custom silicon is becoming an essential part of every hyperscaler’s long-term strategy. Broadcom appears best positioned today thanks to its deep relationships with Google and Meta, while Marvell continues strengthening its foothold with Amazon and other large customers.\nUltimately, investors looking beyond today’s GPU boom may find that the companies quietly designing tomorrow’s AI chips offer just as compelling a long-term opportunity.", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["Morgan Stanley forecasts that Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta will spend over $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027."], "ladder_as_the_judge_is_shown_it": {"object": "ai-capex", "kind": "theme", "question": "How much will Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta spend on AI infrastructure in calendar 2027?", "year": "2027", "due_day": "2028-12-31", "rungs": [{"position": 1, "label": "Below $800 billion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is less than $800 billion."}, {"position": 2, "label": "$800 billion to below $900 billion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $800 billion but less than $900 billion."}, {"position": 3, "label": "$900 billion to below $1 trillion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $900 billion but less than $1 trillion."}, {"position": 4, "label": "$1 trillion to below $1.1 trillion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $1 trillion but less than $1.1 trillion."}, {"position": 5, "label": "$1.1 trillion or more", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $1.1 trillion."}]}, "refused_by_production_check": null}

Time to Walk Away or Double Down?\n\nSince 2023, Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has been the stock to own. It crushed the market in 2023, 2024, and 2025. However, it's not looking so good in 2026.\nAs of this writing, Nvidia is up around 8.7% this year, while the market (as measured by the S&P 500 ) has risen 10.2%. That kind of underperformance is obviously disappointing to the countless Nvidia investors out there, and what makes it even more frustrating is that several other stocks, including rival Advanced Micro Devices , have had phenomenal years.\nSo, is it time to walk away from Nvidia and select a different artificial intelligence (AI) stock? Or is it time to double down on your investment in anticipation of a strong second half? Let's take a look.\nSince the AI arms race began in 2023, Nvidia's GPUs have led the way as the top computing option. Nvidia's GPUs and the products that support them dominate the data center sector and are the top choice for nearly every company involved in AI. This level of dominance helped propel Nvidia to become the world's largest company by market cap, but there are some challenges looming ahead.\nOne threat could come from AI hyperscalers specializing in computing chips, as custom AI chips are starting to become a popular option. However, these chips require a workload to be properly configured to maximize their abilities, and that's not always possible. So, GPUs will remain a popular option.\nWith how bad Nvidia's stock has performed in 2026 (at least compared to the last three years' performance), investors may be surprised to see its rapid growth rates. During its past quarter, Nvidia's revenue increased at an 85% clip. That's not all, either, as Wall Street analysts expect 96% growth during Q2. Nvidia is still rapidly growing, making it a worthy investment, so why has the stock performed so poorly?\nThe most likely reason is skepticism of the AI build-out. The market isn't keen on the AI hyperscalers spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI computing equipment, especially when a viable business hasn't been proven by any generative AI firm yet. {"item": 11, "draw": "stage2-control-d1", "call": 878, "article": "[Item] id gnews:221f52333c8f5e936e515c4d, category T8, author 247wallst.com (analyst), published 2026-07-13, title: Meta Vs. Nvidia: Meta Has Quietly Emerged as the Strongest Mega-Cap Alternative This Summer\n\nMeta Vs. Nvidia: Meta Has Quietly Emerged as the Strongest Mega-Cap Alternative This Summer\nBoth Meta and NVIDIA delivered blowout quarters on the same AI wave, yet investors treated the two stocks very differently this summer. One company quietly flipped its biggest cost line into a potential revenue stream, and that changes the comparison…\nBy Alex Sirois\nNVDA dropped 12% this past month while META gained 7%, as ad pricing power and the new Meta Compute service reframe Meta's AI story.\nMeta Compute converts its massive capex commitment into a recurring revenue stream by renting excess internal AI capacity to enterprises, resembling early AWS.\nMeta's forward P/E of 19 on 33% growth undercuts NVIDIA's 23 multiple, while NVIDIA carries $119B in supply obligations tied to hyperscalers.\nThis graphic visually represents the intense market competition between Meta Platforms and NVIDIA, embodying the rivalry discussed in the accompanying financial analysis. © 24/7 Wall St.\nTwo mega-caps reported blockbuster spring quarters, yet their stocks split hard this summer. Meta Platforms ( NASDAQ: META | META Price Prediction ) posted $56.31 billion in revenue with a huge EPS beat. NVIDIA ( NASDAQ: NVDA ) followed with $81.615 billion and 85.23% growth. Same AI wave. Very different investor treatment lately.\nAds Are Roaring at Meta. Data Centers Are Doing the Work at NVIDIA.\nMeta’s Family of Apps generated $55.91 billion, with ad impressions up 19% and price per ad up 12%. That is real pricing power on a base of 3.56 billion daily users. Mark Zuckerberg framed it plainly: “We had a milestone quarter with strong momentum across our apps and the release of our first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs.” Reality Labs still bled $4.03 billion, a reminder that the AI dream costs real cash.\nNVIDIA’s story is denser. Data Center revenue hit $75.246 billion, up 92%, with Networking exploding 199%. Jensen Huang called it “the largest infrastructure expansion in human history.” Yet zero H20 chips shipped to China this quarter, versus $4.6 billion a year ago. That absence is now baked into forward numbers.\nBuyer of Shovels Turns Seller of Compute\nHere is the twist that reframes the whole quarter. Meta raised 2026 capex to $125 to $145 billion, then quietly launched Meta Compute, a service renting its excess internal AI capacity to external enterprises. That converts a scary cost line into a recurring revenue stream that looks a little like early AWS. NVIDIA, by contrast, carries $119 billion in supply commitments, tying its fortunes to hyperscaler order books .\nThe Next Test Is Whether Meta Compute Actually Prints Revenue\nMeta guided Q2 to $58 to $61 billion. NVIDIA guided to $91.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, explicitly excluding China. I want to see the first disclosed Meta Compute customers, ad pricing durability into the back half, and any softening in hyperscaler order cadence. NVIDIA is down 12.46% over the past month while Meta rallied 7.37% last week. Polymarket traders assign a 0.74 probability that Meta ends 2026 more valuable than OpenAI.\nWhy Meta Screens Better Right Now, With Eyes Open\nOn the metrics, Meta looks like the cleaner setup this summer. A forward multiple near 19 on a business growing 33.1%, with a fresh cloud pivot layered on top, is genuinely rare. NVIDIA remains extraordinary, and the execution story is intact. But when I stack China risk, $119 billion of supply obligations, and a market cap already near $4.79 trillion, the room for error looks thinner. For investors seeking AI exposure with more insulation, Meta offers a differentiated profile. For those prioritizing maximum torque and willing to accept volatility, NVIDIA remains the pure-play.\nBank of America just flagged a hidden revenue engine inside Nvidia that the market is still ignoring, and the numbers suggest Wall Street has been pricing the wrong business this entire time.\nDan Ives Is Still Bullish on Nvidia: ‘We’re in the 3rd Inning of the AI Revolution,’ and Demand Is Outpacing Supply “12 to 1”", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["NVIDIA has $119 billion in supply commitments, linking its results to hyperscaler order books."], "ladder_as_the_judge_is_shown_it": {"object": "NVDA", "kind": "asset", "question": "What amount of NVIDIA purchase commitments will the company report outstanding at its FY2027 year-end?", "year": "FY2027", "due_day": "2027-02-28", "rungs": [{"position": 1, "label": "Strongly bullish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports purchase commitments below $25 billion."}, {"position": 2, "label": "Bullish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports purchase commitments of at least $25 billion and below $50 billion."}, {"position": 3, "label": "Neutral", "condition": "NVIDIA reports purchase commitments of at least $50 billion and below $75 billion."}, {"position": 4, "label": "Bearish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports purchase commitments of at least $75 billion and below $100 billion."}, {"position": 5, "label": "Strongly bearish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports purchase commitments of at least $100 billion."}]}, "refused_by_production_check": null}
{"item": 12, "draw": "stage2-control-d1", "call": 886, "article": "[Item] id gnews:e0e5ab6c2aced8d5a6a688a5, category T8, author 247wallst.com (analyst), published 2026-07-13, title: Broadcom and Marvell Are Bigger Threats to Nvidia Than You Know\n\nBy Rich Duprey\nBroadcom (AVGO) and Marvell (MRVL) design custom AI chips costing between $6 billion and $11 billion per gigawatt, compared to $19 billion for Nvidia GPU racks.\nHyperscalers will spend over $1 trillion on AI next year, with Google alone adding more compute than all four combined did in 2025.\nNvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) remains the undisputed leader of the AI chip market, but leadership and dominance are not the same thing. The next phase of the AI buildout is shifting from buying the fastest hardware available to lowering the cost of operating AI at hyperscale.\nAlphabet ( NASDAQ:GOOG ), Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ), Meta Platforms ( NASDAQ:META ), and Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT ) are all pursuing custom silicon alongside Nvidia’s GPUs because every percentage point of efficiency matters when spending tens of billions of dollars annually on AI infrastructure.\nThat trend doesn’t eliminate Nvidia’s advantage, but it does create a growing opportunity for the companies designing those custom chips—most notably Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) and Marvell Technology ( NASDAQ:MRVL ).\nThe Battle Is Moving From Training to Cost Efficiency\nNvidia still owns AI training. Its GPUs remain the gold standard for developing frontier models, and its CUDA software ecosystem continues to give it a competitive moat. But this is where the market is changing.\nOnce models are trained, they spend years handling inference — answering prompts, generating images, and powering AI applications. Those workloads don’t always require Nvidia’s most powerful processors. They often reward lower costs and higher efficiency instead. That is where application-specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, enter the picture.\nBroadcom has become the leading partner helping hyperscalers build custom AI accelerators, while Marvell has carved out a similar niche with customers including Amazon. Rather than selling chips under their own brands, they help cloud providers design silicon optimized for their own software and infrastructure.\nMorgan Stanley says hyperscalers continue to expand their investments in proprietary silicon to improve total cost of ownership and reduce dependence on merchant GPU suppliers.\nThe opportunity for Broadcom and Marvell is enormous. The analyst says Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta are forecast to spend over $1 trillion on AI infrastructure next year, adding 19.5 gigawatts (GW) of incremental compute capacity. In 2025, they added roughly 6.7 GW. Google alone will add 6.8 GW, or more than the hyperscalers did combined two years ago.\nThe $1 trillion AI infrastructure race is pivoting: training is out, and custom-built efficiency is in. See why the industry's 'Second Act' is making room for new leaders beyond Nvidia.\nThe Economics Are Becoming Harder to Ignore\nThe appeal of custom silicon comes down to dollars. Milk Road AI estimates that building one gigawatt of AI infrastructure using Broadcom- or Marvell-designed ASIC racks cost between $6 billion and $11 billion, compared with roughly $19 billion using Nvidia GB300-based racks. Under Vera Rubin, rack costs jump to $25 billion. It illustrates why hyperscalers are increasingly willing to invest years designing their own chips.\nSurprisingly, this isn’t an either-or decision for hyperscalers. Google continues developing Tensor Processing Units with Broadcom while still purchasing enormous numbers of Nvidia GPUs. Amazon follows a similar strategy with Trainium alongside Nvidia deployments.\nThat diversification gives cloud providers leverage in negotiations while matching the right chip to the right workload.\nNvidia Is Still Winning — But Watch the Suppliers\nGranted, Nvidia is hardly standing still. The company continues expanding beyond GPUs into networking, rack-scale systems, and software while opening technologies such as NVLink Fusion to custom silicon partners — including Marvell itself.\nThat said, investors sometimes underestimate where the fastest incremental growth may occur. Every new custom AI accelerator designed by Google, Meta, Amazon, or another hyperscaler creates another opportunity for Broadcom or Marvell. They benefit whether customers build proprietary chips instead of buying more off-the-shelf processors, and they are standing directly in the path of a massive $1 trillion spending tsunami.\nIn other words, Nvidia remains the king of AI compute, but Broadcom and Marvell are increasingly becoming the architects behind the industry’s second act.\nIn short, investors shouldn’t mistake Nvidia’s dominance for exclusivity. The AI infrastructure market is expanding so rapidly that multiple winners can emerge. Nvidia still commands the premium end of AI computing, particularly for training, but custom silicon is becoming an essential part of every hyperscaler’s long-term strategy. Broadcom appears best positioned today thanks to its deep relationships with Google and Meta, while Marvell continues strengthening its foothold with Amazon and other large customers.\nUltimately, investors looking beyond today’s GPU boom may find that the companies quietly designing tomorrow’s AI chips offer just as compelling a long-term opportunity.", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["Morgan Stanley forecasts that Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta will spend over $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027."], "ladder_as_the_judge_is_shown_it": {"object": "ai-capex", "kind": "theme", "question": "How much will Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta spend on AI infrastructure in calendar 2027?", "year": "2027", "due_day": "2028-12-31", "rungs": [{"position": 1, "label": "Below $800 billion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is less than $800 billion."}, {"position": 2, "label": "$800 billion to below $900 billion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $800 billion but less than $900 billion."}, {"position": 3, "label": "$900 billion to below $1 trillion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $900 billion but less than $1 trillion."}, {"position": 4, "label": "$1 trillion to below $1.1 trillion", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $1 trillion but less than $1.1 trillion."}, {"position": 5, "label": "$1.1 trillion or more", "condition": "Combined AI infrastructure spending is at least $1.1 trillion."}]}, "refused_by_production_check": null}

Meanwhile, Firmus is building a DSX-aligned campus in Batam, Indonesia, that’s expected to scale to 360 MW and house up to 170,000 Nvidia GPUs.\nNvidia has spent much of the last year funnelling cash directly to its customers, including a $30 billion participation in OpenAI's $110 billion funding round and backing for xAI's $20 billion Colossus 2 financing , arrangements that drew repeated circular financing criticism. The new model inverts that: rather than investing capital that returns as GPU orders, Nvidia extends credit support and collects a royalty on its partners’ sales for years afterward.\nThat royalty also ties a slice of Nvidia's income to utilization instead of hardware sales. If partner clouds can’t keep racks rented, the usage-linked stream shrinks, a live concern given the depreciation pressure already building on operators paying off hardware that Nvidia refreshes pretty much every year.\nRevenue? All these startups are or will be horribly unprofitable, the lengths one takes to ensure they can keep buying leather jackets.", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["Nvidia announced a model combining hardware sales with an ongoing percentage of partner AI-cloud revenue generated using its hardware; the revenue-share percentage was not disclosed.", "Sharon AI disclosed an agreement running for six years covering 72 MW of new Australian data-center capacity built to Nvidia's DSX design, with capacity for up to 40,000 Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs."], "ladder_as_the_judge_is_shown_it": {"object": "NVDA", "kind": "asset", "question": "What total amount of financing commitments and capacity backstops to customers and partners will NVIDIA report outstanding at its FY2027 year-end?", "year": "FY2027", "due_day": "2027-02-28", "rungs": [{"position": 1, "label": "Strongly bullish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports less than $1 billion outstanding."}, {"position": 2, "label": "Bullish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports at least $1 billion but less than $5 billion outstanding."}, {"position": 3, "label": "Neutral", "condition": "NVIDIA reports at least $5 billion but less than $10 billion outstanding."}, {"position": 4, "label": "Bearish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports at least $10 billion but less than $20 billion outstanding."}, {"position": 5, "label": "Strongly bearish", "condition": "NVIDIA reports at least $20 billion outstanding."}]}, "refused_by_production_check": null}
{"item": 17, "draw": "stage2-control-d3", "call": 142, "article": "[Item] id gnews:1e7a9c953f3ad70093b67ae4, category T7, author datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com (media), published 2026-07-04, title: Nvidia introduces revenue-sharing model for AI cloud financing\n\nNvidia introduces revenue-sharing model for AI cloud financing\nNvidia has launched a revenue-sharing financing model aimed at AI cloud providers, facilitating access to its computing infrastructure. This initiative is designed to support startups and enterprises in scaling AI operations.\nNvidia launches a revenue-sharing financing model for AI cloud providers.\nThe model aims to facilitate access to large-scale AI compute for startups and enterprises.\nSharon AI and Firmus are early adopters of the financing structure.\nThe initiative reflects a shift in the AI market towards production inference.\nNvidia has unveiled a revenue-sharing financing model to assist AI cloud providers in acquiring its computing infrastructure, thereby enhancing access to large-scale AI compute for startups, enterprises, researchers, and regional providers.\nThis model is particularly relevant as the market transitions from model development to production inference, where computing systems operate continuously to deliver AI outputs at scale.\nUnder this financing structure, AI cloud operators can procure Nvidia infrastructure with credit support, with revenue sharing linked to the cloud services sold based on that capacity.\nNvidia will receive its standard product revenue from infrastructure sales, in addition to a share of the cloud revenue generated from the supported capacity. This approach offers AI cloud operators a viable means to finance large installations, which have traditionally been challenging to fund, especially for emerging companies lacking the balance sheet strength typically required for capital-intensive projects.\nThe initiative reflects a significant shift in the AI market, where demand is increasingly focused not only on training large models but also on running them in production for enterprises, software providers, and AI-native businesses that require constant access to computing resources for inference, fine-tuning, and related workloads.\nTwo companies are among the first to collaborate with Nvidia under this model. Sharon AI plans to deploy up to 40,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs, while Firmus is developing a DSX AI factory campus in Batam, Indonesia, which is expected to scale to 360 megawatts and accommodate up to 170,000 Nvidia GPUs. These projects exemplify the scale of infrastructure Nvidia aims to facilitate through this financing model, which is linked to future usage rather than relying solely on conventional long-term commitments.\nNvidia describes these facilities as DSX AI factories tailored to customer demand in various regions. For users of AI infrastructure, this model promises faster access to computing capacity, eliminating delays associated with site selection, power procurement, construction, and hardware installation typical of traditional buildouts.\nAccess to compute has been a persistent constraint across the AI sector, with many emerging companies struggling to secure the necessary capital to lock in supply, even when demand is evident. Nvidia's strategy aims to alleviate this bottleneck by aligning its financial interests more closely with cloud providers serving these customers.\nAs the AI landscape evolves, suppliers like Nvidia are adapting to the changing economics of AI services. With more companies transitioning from experimental phases to commercial products, there is a growing need for computing supply that can scale with usage while maintaining flexibility in payment structures during the shift from pilot projects to full deployment.\nNvidia highlighted the needs of model builders, inference providers, and enterprises requiring immediate cloud access for various AI-related tasks. The company also pointed to AI-native businesses such as Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Together AI as examples of where demand is heading.\nThese entities depend on reliable access to accelerated computing as customer usage increases, often requiring more adaptable commercial arrangements than traditional data center buildouts or fixed infrastructure commitments allow.\nFor Nvidia, this model not only creates a recurring income stream tied to the usage of supported cloud capacity but also deepens its involvement in the AI cloud market as competition intensifies among providers aiming to serve developers, digital-native companies, and established enterprises.\nSharon AI's co-founder and CEO, James Manning, described the agreement as a milestone for the company's plans, stating, \"This strategic collaboration with NVIDIA marks a pivotal moment in Sharon AI's mission to deliver sovereign, large-scale AI compute infrastructure.\"\nFirmus co-CEO Tim Rosenfield emphasized the importance of infrastructure access for globally competitive AI businesses, noting, \"AI-native companies need access to scalable, energy- and cost-efficient compute infrastructure to compete globally.\"\nHe added that the Firmus AI cloud is building a NVIDIA DSX-aligned AI factory to enable more customers to access the compute necessary for building and scaling AI.", {"item": 18, "draw": "stage2-control-d3", "call": 208, "article": "[Item] id gnews:98a4e8ff0c0260d8dc9e531d, category T7, author datacenterdynamics.com (media), published 2026-07-06, title: Nvidia pushes Kyber release to 2028 following manufacturing concerns – report\n\nBy Charlotte Trueman\nNvidia has delayed production of its Kyber rack-scale architecture by more than 12 months, pushing its release date to 2028, SemiAnalysis has reported.\nThe Kyber server cabinets, which have been designed to house 144 Rubin Ultra GPUs connected via the company’s NVLink 7 Switch, had originally been slated for release in 2027.\nKyber allows GPUs to be mounted in compute trays that sit vertically rather than horizontally, a design that Nvidia has described as being “like books on a shelf,” and which reportedly boosts density and reduces latency.\nHowever, the research firm claimed that issues in manufacturing the printed circuit board (PCB) midplane that connects the modules together have caused the setback.\n“Kyber NVL144 rack architecture has been delayed to 2028 as the PCB midplane remains challenging from a manufacturability standpoint,” SemiAnalysis said, adding that Nvidia’s alternative plan, which involved placing two Oberon racks back-to-back in order to achieve a similar power output, has also been scrapped after cloud companies and hyperscalers pushed back against its “odd design and heavy operational burden.”\nThe manufacturing issues will also impact the planned NVL576 system, which connects 8x Oberon racks over CPO between the NVSwitches, meaning that the system will also likely be delayed or limited to small volumes, the firm noted. All this leaves Nvidia with “no proven solution to expand the scale-up world size for Rubin Ultra,” SemiAnalysis said.\nFirst announced at Nvidia’s GTC conference in 2025, Nvidia has previously said the liquid-cooled Kyber racks will offer a 4x performance improvement over its Blackwell NVL72 system – also known as Oberon – and consume some 600kW.\nThe news comes a week after SemiAnalysis separately reported that Nvidia had canceled the four-die Rubin Ultra design in favor of the two-chiplet design, also due to “manufacturing execution concerns.” The two-die offering will deliver around half the performance of the four-die Rubin Ultra.\nIn response to a request for comment from DCD regarding the Kyber claims, a spokesperson for Nvidia said: \"Our roadmap is intact.\"", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["SemiAnalysis reported that Nvidia’s Kyber NVL144 rack architecture had been delayed to 2028 because of PCB midplane manufacturability challenges; it had originally been slated for release in 2027.", "SemiAnalysis reported that Nvidia scrapped its alternative plan to place two Oberon racks back-to-back after cloud companies and hyperscalers objected to the design and operational burden.", "SemiAnalysis said manufacturing issues could delay Nvidia’s planned NVL576 system or limit it to small volumes.", "Nvidia said its product roadmap remained intact in response to the report about Kyber’s delay."], "ladder_as_the_judge_is_shown_it": {"object": "NVDA", "kind": "asset", "question": "Will NVIDIA begin shipping its Rubin Ultra generation in Kyber NVL144 racks by December 31, 2027?", "year": "2027", "due_day": "2027-12-31", "rungs": [{"position": 1, "label": "Yes", "condition": "NVIDIA has begun shipping Rubin Ultra in Kyber NVL144 racks by December 31, 2027."}, {"position": 2, "label": "No", "condition": "NVIDIA has not begun shipping Rubin Ultra in Kyber NVL144 racks by December 31, 2027."}]}, "refused_by_production_check": null}

clean-arch/step4-2026-11-10/reference/reader-codex-2.stream:20:{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_9","type":"command_execution","command":"/opt/homebrew/bin/zsh -lc "python3 -c 'import json; p=json.load(open(\"/Users/lchingen/hivemind/clean-arch/step4-2026-11-10/reference/packet.json\")); [print(json.dumps(x,ensure_ascii=False)) for x in p[24:27]]'"","aggregated_output":"{"item": 25, "draw": "stage2-control-d4", "call": 105, "article": "[Item] id gnews:9e0d5b0d6b3e603c60340128, category T7, author mlq.ai (media), published 2026-07-03, title: Nvidia Launches GPU Backstop Financing Model, Takes Cut of Cloud Revenue From Neocloud Partners\n\nNvidia will act as a financial backstop for neocloud GPU deployments, agreeing to rent back unused GPUs at a fixed rate in exchange for a share of cloud revenue generated on that capacity [1]\nSharon AI plans to deploy up to 40,000 Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs in Australia under a six-year agreement; Firmus Technologies targets up to 170,000 GPUs in a 360MW DSX-aligned facility in Batam, Indonesia [1] [3]\nThe revenue-share percentage was not disclosed; Nvidia declined to provide details beyond its blog post co-authored by CFO Colette Kress [3]\nThe structure gives Nvidia both standard hardware revenue and a recurring, usage-linked earnings stream — a shift from pure equipment sales toward platform-level economics [1]\nSHAZ shares fell 14.2% to $67.91 on July 3; NVDA dipped 1.4% to $194.83 on a $4.7 trillion market cap [5]\nNvidia on July 1 unveiled a new financing vehicle it calls the \"AI Compute Partnership,\" under which the chipmaker acts as a financial backstop for neocloud customers' GPU deployments and, in return, takes a recurring share of the cloud revenue those GPUs generate [1] . The program's first two adopters are Sharon AI (NASDAQ: SHAZ), an Australian sovereign-cloud provider planning up to 40,000 Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs, and Firmus Technologies, which is building a 360MW campus in Batam, Indonesia, targeting up to 170,000 Nvidia GPUs [1] [2] .\nThe arrangement creates a dual revenue stream for Nvidia: the company collects standard product revenue from the GPU sale, then earns an additional usage-linked cut of the cloud services those chips power. Nvidia described the model as providing \"economic alignment with a revenue-sharing and credit-support model\" in a blog post co-authored by CFO Colette Kress [1] [3] . The specific revenue-share percentage was not disclosed, and Nvidia declined to offer further details beyond the blog post [3] .\nThe backstop mechanism works by Nvidia agreeing to rent back unused GPUs at a fixed rate, effectively de-risking lender exposure and making it easier for smaller cloud operators to secure capital for large GPU deployments [1] [3] . The structure echoes — but formalizes — earlier arrangements in which Nvidia provided demand guarantees to help neoclouds like CoreWeave and Lambda raise billions in debt financing [1] .\nUnder the AI Compute Partnership, Nvidia guarantees a floor utilization rate on deployed GPUs. If a neocloud partner's customer demand falls short, Nvidia commits to renting the idle capacity at a predetermined rate, absorbing the downside risk that would otherwise sit with lenders or equity investors [1] [3] . In exchange, Nvidia earns both its standard product revenue from the hardware sale and a recurring, usage-linked share of the cloud revenue generated on the supported capacity [1] .\nThe model addresses a persistent bottleneck in the neocloud sector: smaller operators often have customer demand in hand but cannot secure financing quickly enough to build infrastructure, because lenders view GPU residual values as uncertain [4] . By backstopping idle capacity, Nvidia effectively underwrites the asset, making GPU clusters more bankable. The company framed the program as accelerating 'adoption of Nvidia platforms among the high-growth, high-conviction AI native sector' [1] .\nSharon AI, which listed on the Nasdaq in February 2026 via a $125 million IPO, is deploying up to 40,000 Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs under a six-year agreement with Nvidia [2] [6] . The company raised an additional $1.6 billion in private placement in June 2026 to fund its Nvidia-based AI factory and has partnered with VAST Data for 600PB of storage infrastructure supporting roughly 100,000 GPUs across its sovereign cloud operations in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region [6] .\nFirmus Technologies, a private company, is constructing a campus in Batam, Indonesia, built to Nvidia's DGX SuperPOD (DSX) reference architecture specifications. The facility is expected to scale to 360MW and house up to 170,000 Nvidia GPUs [1] [3] . Both operators plan to serve AI-native companies including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Together AI, as well as enterprise inference workloads [4] .\nThe AI Compute Partnership represents a structural evolution in Nvidia's business model. Prior to this formalization, Nvidia had provided demand guarantees and customer referrals to help neoclouds raise debt — CoreWeave secured $6.3 billion and Lambda $1.5 billion through arrangements in which Nvidia played a supporting role [1] . The new model makes Nvidia's financial participation explicit, with the company now directly sharing in its customers' cloud economics.\nThe shift creates a recurring revenue layer on top of Nvidia's hardware sales, potentially smoothing earnings volatility tied to GPU refresh cycles. Analysts have drawn comparisons to GE Capital's equipment financing model, noting both the upside of recurring income and the counterparty risk if neocloud operators face financial stress [4] . Nvidia's blog post positioned the arrangement as providing 'a recurring, usage-linked earnings stream' that diversifies its revenue beyond one-time chip sales [1] .\nNvidia shares traded at $194.83 on July 3, down 1.4% on the session, on a market capitalization of approximately $4.7 trillion. The stock is up 4.5% year-to-date and 22.3% over the past twelve months [5] . The muted reaction suggests investors are still parsing the margin implications of revenue-sharing arrangements versus the benefits of demand-side de-risking.\nSharon AI shares fell sharply, dropping 14.2% to $67.91 on volume of 2.6 million shares. The stock, which IPO'd at roughly $16.55 in February, had rallied to a high of $97.48 in June before the pullback [5] . Firmus Technologies is privately held and does not have a public ticker.\nThe financing model keeps a broader ecosystem of independent GPU cloud providers alive rather than concentrating AI compute inside the hyperscalers — a strategic imperative for Nvidia, which benefits from having multiple distribution channels for its hardware [3] [4] . By making GPU clusters more financeable, Nvidia may accelerate buildout timelines for operators that would otherwise face 12- to 18-month fundraising cycles.\nThe structure also gives Nvidia optionality: in a demand downturn, the company gains access to GPU capacity it can deploy for its own inference services or sublease, effectively building a buffer inventory at customer expense. {"item": 26, "draw": "stage2-control-d4", "call": 140, "article": "[Item] id gnews:1e7a9c953f3ad70093b67ae4, category T7, author datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com (media), published 2026-07-04, title: Nvidia introduces revenue-sharing model for AI cloud financing\n\nNvidia introduces revenue-sharing model for AI cloud financing\nNvidia has launched a revenue-sharing financing model aimed at AI cloud providers, facilitating access to its computing infrastructure. This initiative is designed to support startups and enterprises in scaling AI operations.\nNvidia launches a revenue-sharing financing model for AI cloud providers.\nThe model aims to facilitate access to large-scale AI compute for startups and enterprises.\nSharon AI and Firmus are early adopters of the financing structure.\nThe initiative reflects a shift in the AI market towards production inference.\nNvidia has unveiled a revenue-sharing financing model to assist AI cloud providers in acquiring its computing infrastructure, thereby enhancing access to large-scale AI compute for startups, enterprises, researchers, and regional providers.\nThis model is particularly relevant as the market transitions from model development to production inference, where computing systems operate continuously to deliver AI outputs at scale.\nUnder this financing structure, AI cloud operators can procure Nvidia infrastructure with credit support, with revenue sharing linked to the cloud services sold based on that capacity.\nNvidia will receive its standard product revenue from infrastructure sales, in addition to a share of the cloud revenue generated from the supported capacity. This approach offers AI cloud operators a viable means to finance large installations, which have traditionally been challenging to fund, especially for emerging companies lacking the balance sheet strength typically required for capital-intensive projects.\nThe initiative reflects a significant shift in the AI market, where demand is increasingly focused not only on training large models but also on running them in production for enterprises, software providers, and AI-native businesses that require constant access to computing resources for inference, fine-tuning, and related workloads.\nTwo companies are among the first to collaborate with Nvidia under this model. Sharon AI plans to deploy up to 40,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GB300 GPUs, while Firmus is developing a DSX AI factory campus in Batam, Indonesia, which is expected to scale to 360 megawatts and accommodate up to 170,000 Nvidia GPUs. These projects exemplify the scale of infrastructure Nvidia aims to facilitate through this financing model, which is linked to future usage rather than relying solely on conventional long-term commitments.\nNvidia describes these facilities as DSX AI factories tailored to customer demand in various regions. For users of AI infrastructure, this model promises faster access to computing capacity, eliminating delays associated with site selection, power procurement, construction, and hardware installation typical of traditional buildouts.\nAccess to compute has been a persistent constraint across the AI sector, with many emerging companies struggling to secure the necessary capital to lock in supply, even when demand is evident. Nvidia's strategy aims to alleviate this bottleneck by aligning its financial interests more closely with cloud providers serving these customers.\nAs the AI landscape evolves, suppliers like Nvidia are adapting to the changing economics of AI services. With more companies transitioning from experimental phases to commercial products, there is a growing need for computing supply that can scale with usage while maintaining flexibility in payment structures during the shift from pilot projects to full deployment.\nNvidia highlighted the needs of model builders, inference providers, and enterprises requiring immediate cloud access for various AI-related tasks. The company also pointed to AI-native businesses such as Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Together AI as examples of where demand is heading.\nThese entities depend on reliable access to accelerated computing as customer usage increases, often requiring more adaptable commercial arrangements than traditional data center buildouts or fixed infrastructure commitments allow.\nFor Nvidia, this model not only creates a recurring income stream tied to the usage of supported cloud capacity but also deepens its involvement in the AI cloud market as competition intensifies among providers aiming to serve developers, digital-native companies, and established enterprises.\nSharon AI's co-founder and CEO, James Manning, described the agreement as a milestone for the company's plans, stating, \"This strategic collaboration with NVIDIA marks a pivotal moment in Sharon AI's mission to deliver sovereign, large-scale AI compute infrastructure.\"\nFirmus co-CEO Tim Rosenfield emphasized the importance of infrastructure access for globally competitive AI businesses, noting, \"AI-native companies need access to scalable, energy- and cost-efficient compute infrastructure to compete globally.\"\nHe added that the Firmus AI cloud is building a NVIDIA DSX-aligned AI factory to enable more customers to access the compute necessary for building and scaling AI.", "statements_the_question_was_opened_from": ["NVIDIA launched a financing model for AI cloud providers in which operators can procure NVIDIA infrastructure with credit support, and NVIDIA receives product revenue plus a share of cloud revenue generated from the supported capacity; {"item": 27, "draw": "stage2-control-d4", "call": 206, "article": "[Item] id gnews:54aa9ce326115cedf8857512, category T7, author theberkshireedge.com (media), published 2026-07-06, title: CAPITAL IDEAS: The lag 7 — Is Micron the new Nvidia?\n\nMy rule of thumb, which I borrowed from DataTrek, is that a double is a bubble. If a company’s stock price doubles within a year, there is a good chance the price has advanced much faster than the fundamentals.\nBig Tech leadership is shifting. The Magnificent 7 and Broadcom weakened in June, while the broader market held up better than expected and Micron surged.\nInvestors should respect both the opportunity and the risk. Micron’s growth, margins, and role in AI memory are impressive, but its rapid stock rise has started to look bubble-like.\nBottom line: Micron is not the new Nvidia, but it is a serious AI beneficiary. The stock may still have long-term potential, but position size and diversification matter more after such a huge run.\nTwo years ago, the darling of Wall Street was Nvidia , the technology company that sells graphics processing units (GPUs) used by artificial intelligence companies.\nThat was two years ago. As Barron’s recently referenced, Micron is the new Nvidia.\nMicron’s stock is up about 855 percent in the last 12 months, while Nvidia traded down over 15 percent from its June 2, 2026, high. In fairness, June 2026 was a harsh month for many technology stocks. Nvidia’s stock was down about five percent in June; however, Micron’s stock shook off the June swoon and was up about 19 percent.\nIt’s not just Nvidia that got smashed in June. Nearly all of the so-called Magnificent 7 stocks, plus Broadcom, are below their respective 50-day moving averages (Tesla being the exception), a sign that price weakness is becoming a trend. Those eight stocks account for about 34 percent of the S&P 500; each was down roughly three percent to 17 percent in June.\nDespite over one-third of the S&P 500’s market capitalization taking it on the chin in June, the index itself was down only about one percent and remained around its 50-day moving average. That is because the next 492 stocks were up an average of two percent.\n(To briefly address the concentration, two years ago, that was often cited as a major risk to the stock market. In November 2024, the eight largest companies at the time represented 33.5 percent of the S&P 500—nearly identical to today. I wrote then, “It is OK for the S&P 500 to have a handful of companies representing a large percentage of the index.” I don’t have any reason to feel differently today; the index is up about 25 percent since then.)\nAs you will recall, the S&P 500 is market-cap weighted, and it was down about one percent in June. In contrast, the equal-weighted S&P 500 index, often represented by the RSP ETF, was up by about 1.9 percent. The correlation between market-cap and the equal-weighted S&P 500 is at a record low.\nBased on the performance of the biggest eight stocks, it is no wonder that the S&P 500 stalled out after hitting a high on June 2. Based on the performance of the other 492 stocks, it is no wonder that the index was only down about one percent from its recent high as of the end of June, which is not a lot.\nInterestingly, the S&P 500 is up about 9.5 percent year to date, but over the same period, the forward price-to-earnings ratio has contracted nearly 10 percent. That is because earnings of the companies in that index have been incredible, with roughly an 18 percent growth rate for the first half of 2026, and Q2 expected to be above 20 percent.\nThat trend—rising stock prices and simultaneously improving valuations—is very bullish. I have doubts that the earnings growth rate can continue at that pace, but it is not impossible. I mean, it just happened, so we know it is not impossible.\nFor earnings to keep improving, we need 1) lower oil prices (which seems to be happening), 2) the AI-related infrastructure buildout to continue (I suspect it will through the next 12 months), and 3) interest rates to stay where they are, or go lower (but the futures market says they will go higher). So, two out of three ain’t bad, and it is probably enough to keep the economy from slipping into a recession and keep the stock market from crashing. But two out of three probably isn’t enough for stocks to rocket higher either.\nIt seems worth staying invested, even if the S&P pullback hits double digits in the short term. Unfortunately, that short-term pain is the entry fee for the potential of long-term rewards.\nDespite the weakness in large technology stocks, Micron has had enough positive performance to push it into the coveted trillion-dollar club. Apple was the first company to reach a $1 trillion market capitalization, and at the time, many people thought it was so outlandish a number that it would signal a market top. Apple hit $1 trillion in 2018; now there are 17 companies in the trillion-dollar club.\nIs Micron the new Nvidia?\nTwo years ago, investors kept asking if it was too late to buy Nvidia . I wrote about this on July 22, 2024. Since then, Nvidia’s stock is up about 55 percent, compared to the S&P 500’s 32 percent. Micron, though, has soared about 937 percent since then.\nMicron makes memory and storage chips that help computers, phones, cars, data centers, and AI systems store and quickly access data.\nMake no mistake about it, memory stocks are starting to feel bubble-like. Micron has been one of the best-performing stocks in the S&P 500 this year, and after its latest earnings report, the stock jumped nearly 16 percent in a single day. Other memory chip companies, such as SK Hynix and Samsung, have also experienced massive runups. When an entire corner of the market starts moving like a meme stock, investors should slow down and ask whether the story has gotten ahead of the math. My rule of thumb, which I borrowed from DataTrek , is that a double is a bubble. If a company’s stock price doubles within a year, there is a good chance the price has advanced much faster than the fundamentals.\nI invested in the Invesco AI and Next Gen Software ETF (NOT an investment recommendation), which had 27 percent of its weighting in memory stocks. Each of the memory stocks in that ETF has way more than doubled. It has been a wild ride up, but I worry that it is on the precipice of a decline. But let’s look at Micron to think about whether a decline is warranted and, if so, if it might be short term or permanent.\nIn Micron’s case, the math is stunning. For its third fiscal quarter of 2026, Micron reported revenue of $41.46 billion. One year earlier, revenue was $9.30 billion. That is roughly 346 percent revenue growth. GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) net income was $28.24 billion, compared with $1.89 billion a year ago. Micron’s gross margin was 84.6 percent, up from 37.7 percent a year earlier, and its operating margin was 80.4 percent, up from 23.3 percent. That is actual money hitting the income statement now.\nThe new Micron is still cyclical, but investors may view the durability of its earnings more favorably because artificial intelligence needs a lot of memory.\nA graphics processor (like those designed by Nvidia) powers the AI data center, but memory is just as important. Large AI models need to move huge amounts of data quickly. If data doesn’t reach the processor fast enough, it has to wait, which can be costly.\nHigh-bandwidth memory (HBM) sits close to the AI accelerator and feeds it data at high speed. Storage also matters because training, checkpointing, data retrieval, and inference all require huge amounts of fast, reliable memory and storage infrastructure.\nThat is why Nvidia’s success is spilling over into Micron. Nvidia remains the king of AI chips. Micron’s latest revenue growth was about 346 percent, compared with Nvidia’s 85 percent. Micron’s GAAP gross margin was 84.6 percent, compared with Nvidia’s 74.9 percent. Micron’s operating margin was 80.4 percent, compared with Nvidia’s roughly 66 percent. Nvidia still earns more dollars. Micron is growing faster right now and, at least in the latest quarter, is showing even fatter margins.\nThat is why investors are watching closely.\nThe broader capital-spending backdrop supports the rally. Goldman Sachs estimates annual AI infrastructure capital expenditures could reach $765 billion in 2026 and grow to $1.6 trillion by 2031, with cumulative spending of about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031. That spending includes chips, data centers, power, cooling, networking, and the other plumbing required to run AI at scale. Memory is one of those essential pieces of plumbing.\nUnfortunately, the AI boom is not just pushing up prices for the winners. It could also raise costs for everyone else. A shortage of memory might affect the prices of consumer electronics.\nApple said it can no longer absorb the surge in memory and storage costs and announced price increases for some Macs and iPads, citing higher memory costs. When Micron’s profit margins grow, it means higher costs for others. If memory companies earn more, then device makers, server makers, cloud providers, and eventually consumers could end up paying more for electronics.\nSo, is Micron the new Nvidia?\nMemory is now a key asset in the AI economy. But when a stock doubles or more, the risk goes up, even if the business is strong. However, ignoring Micron just because it has risen sharply could be the same mistake many made with Nvidia. Position size and diversification are important.\nNvidia is still the main name in AI, at least until companies like OpenAI and Anthropic go public. Micron and other memory chip makers are becoming key players in this space. I’d say Micron is not the new Nvidia, just a new opportunity (talk to your financial advisor before making any investment). But again, mind your position size and diversification: If you own the S&P 500 index, Micron already accounts for about 1.7 percent of that investment.\nAllen Harris is an owner of Berkshire Money Management in Great Barrington and Dalton, managing more than $1 billion of investments.
